keyVerseText: Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side? thou hast blessed the work of his hands, and his substance is increased in the land. substance: or, cattle
rootMeaning: The Hebrew verb שׂוּךְ (sûwk) is a primitive root that fundamentally conveys the idea of fencing or hedging in. Its core sense involves entwining or enclosing something to form a protective or restraining boundary. This literal sense of creating a physical barrier enriches the English glosses such as 'fence' or 'hedge' by emphasizing the intentional act of securing or safeguarding through enclosure.
usageInScripture: The word שׂוּךְ appears three times in Scripture, consistently conveying the concept of forming a hedge or fence around something. Its translations include phrases like 'Hast not thou made an hedge,' 'and hast fenced,' and 'Therefore behold I will hedge,' indicating both protective and obstructive uses. This consistency reveals that the term is used both to describe divine protection and to signal restriction or obstruction, depending on context.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שׂוּךְ deepens our appreciation of God's providential care and sovereignty. The image of God 'hedging' or 'fencing' about His people underscores His role as protector who surrounds His children with divine barriers against harm. At the same time, the notion of hedging can imply God’s authority to restrain or limit, reminding believers that His protection includes both blessing and discipline. This dual aspect highlights the intimate and active involvement of God in the lives of His people, guarding their well-being and guiding their paths according to His perfect will.
keyVerseReflection: In Job 1:10, the phrase 'Hast not thou made an hedge about him, and about his house, and about all that he hath on every side?' uses שׂוּךְ to vividly depict God's comprehensive protection over Job. The word conveys that God has intentionally enclosed Job and his possessions with a protective boundary, emphasizing divine safeguarding. This enriches the verse by portraying God's blessing not just as favor but as a tangible, surrounding defense that preserves and increases what He has entrusted to His servant.
